1. Core Clinical Tension: A 38-year-old male native of Ivory Coast residing in Europe presented with subacute asymmetric paraparesis and neurogenic bladder. Spine MRI demonstrated an expansile, heterogeneously enhancing intramedullary mass at D4-D5 with surrounding edema, which grossly and histologically was initially mistaken for a high-grade intramedullary glioma, before parasitological review demonstrated medullary schistosomiasis.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission clinical encounter ends following emergency neurological evaluation, baseline blood work (absence of peripheral eosinophilia, normal ESR), and spinal MRI demonstrating the D4-D5 cord enlargement, immediately prior to D3-D5 laminotomy, myelotomy, and tissue excision.
3. Differential Distinctions: High-grade intramedullary spinal cord glioma was the dominant clinical and radiologic diagnosis, even suspected on preliminary intraoperative frozen section, but excluded by definitive histopathology revealing parasitic granulomas without neoplastic glial cells. Transverse myelitis was argued against by normal CSF biochemistry without pleocytosis. Definitive diagnosis of spinal schistosomiasis was confirmed by histopathological demonstration of Schistosoma eggs containing miracidia and adult worm fragments, corroborated by positive indirect hemagglutination serology.
case_prompt:
A 38-year-old male, native of Ivory Coast and living in Portugal for the past 6 years, presented to the emergency department with a 1-month history of progressive motor weakness in his lower extremities and neurogenic bladder dysfunction manifest as urinary retention and overflow incontinence requiring urethral catheterization.

On neurological examination, he exhibited asymmetric spastic paraparesis with a motor strength grade of 3/5 in the right lower extremity and 4/5 in the left lower extremity. Deep tendon reflexes in the lower limbs were diminished bilaterally. Sensory examination revealed a sharp sensory level at D10. The remainder of the neurological examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory evaluation revealed absence of peripheral blood eosinophilia, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine documented moderate and diffuse enlargement of the spinal cord in the D4–D5 region, characterized by central non-homogeneous T2 hypersignal and heterogeneous contrast enhancement with a granular pattern after intravenous gadolinium administration.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered the primary provisional diagnosis due to progressive subacute paraparesis, sensory level, cord enlargement with granular gadolinium enhancement on MRI, and gross appearance during myelotomy; preliminary histopathologic review even suggested glioma, but definitive analysis demonstrated parasitic granulomatous inflammation with eggs and adult worms rather than malignant glial proliferation.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Preliminary histopathologic review found the lesion to be suggestive of a high grade glioma. That result being known, after gross total removal, the dura was closed with 3/0 vycril suture, and the laminae were not put in place as previously planned in order to allow lesion growth without cord compression.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given the subacute sensory level at D10, paraparesis, and intramedullary T2 cord expansion; ruled out by completely normal cerebrospinal fluid analysis without pleocytosis or protein elevation, and by the focal granulomatous mass identified at surgery.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The CSF biochemical analysis was normal, with no pleiocytosis, no eosinophils, normal protein, and glucose levels.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Microscopic analysis of the excised spinal cord mass demonstrated chronic granulomatous inflammation with eosinophils containing numerous Schistosoma eggs (some with intact miracidia) and adult worm fragments, confirmed by positive indirect hemagglutination serology, with significant motor recovery following surgical excision, praziquantel, and corticosteroids.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The diagnosis of schistosomiasis was based solely on the demonstration of eggs and adult worm in the granuloma supplied for histopathology review [Figure 4], and later confirmed by positivity in serological tests hemagglutination... On histopathological examination, the spinal cord tissue showed edema, demyelination, and a chronic inflammatory cellular infiltrate with some eosinophils. Numerous eggs were observed, some containing miracidia with intact nuclei and a few showed calcifications.

editor_comments: Spinal cord schistosomiasis is an uncommon but devastating ectopic manifestation of schistosomiasis that frequently mimics intramedullary tumors. Systemic signs like peripheral eosinophilia or urinary/stool eggs are frequently absent, requiring histopathological or serological confirmation.
